There's an old joke that every time Apple unveils a new iPhone Pro, they say it's "the best iPhone we've ever made," as if that's supposed to be some kind of惊喜.

Specifically, we expect next year will finally move toward that "all-glass" vision, putting a decade of incremental improvements to rest……

The Evolution of the iPhone Pro Line

If you line up the iPhone 12 Pro through the 16 Pro, I think most people would struggle to tell them apart at a glance—except for the switch from the notch to the Dynamic Island in 2022. As for the iPhone 17 Pro, there's even less to identify it by, mainly its elongated camera module and that "cosmic orange" colour.

Of course, each generation brings new features, but to be fair, unless one of them happens to be particularly useful to you, you really need to skip at least two or three generations before it's worth it to upgrade for a noticeable improvement in experience.

None of this is meant as a criticism of Apple. The fact is that smartphones are mature technology now, at least at the level of conventional design. You're not going to see huge differences between adjacent generations, because year after year there's just not much room left to improve.

Apple is now starting to experiment with different designs—first, of course, the iPhone Air and the iPhone Duo—and we expect another significant design leap next year, with that 20th-anniversary model.

How Apple will position next year's design is still a bit unclear. Previous rumours said it would be a standalone model, not part of the iPhone 19 Pro lineup, but other reports suggest it will be next year's Pro model. There's also the question of whether Apple will use consecutive numbering, or skip a number to mark the milestone—so it might end up being called the iPhone 20 Pro.

For my part, I expect it to be the new iPhone Pro design, regardless of whether Apple calls it the 19 or 20. If so, then the iPhone 18 Pro will be the final version of this six- or seven-year look.

I'll start by skipping two generations from the iPhone 16 Pro, so I'll list what each year's model brings me. I'll skip improvements that are completely irrelevant to me or that I have absolutely no use for, like going from a 6-core GPU to a 7-core GPU, and GenLock.

Features Carried Over from the iPhone 17 Pro

  • Center Stage front camera (photos and video calls)
  • Ultra-stabilised video
  • Dual-camera simultaneous recording
  • Telephoto lens upgraded from 5x to 8x
  • Telephoto sensor upgraded from 12 MP to 48 MP
  • ProRes RAW video
  • Longer battery life
  • Faster charging speeds

New Features of the iPhone 18 Pro

  • Larger maximum aperture on the main camera
  • Variable aperture on the main camera
  • Pro-grade camera controls (aperture, shutter speed, white balance, histogram)
  • Third-generation Photographic Styles
  • Intelligent subject tracking
  • Cinematic mode added to standard video
  • Tap-to-zoom and rotate gestures added to the front camera
  • Smaller Dynamic Island, capable of displaying three Live Activities simultaneously
  • (Even) longer battery life
  • (Even) faster charging speeds

My Personal... Focus Features

For me personally, at this stage I'm mainly paying attention to five features.

Variable aperture lens

Although the showstopper is the variable aperture lens, as I've said before, don't expect too much from it. The maximum aperture is only slightly larger, and the sensor is still on the small side, so I'm not expecting a huge difference in shallow depth-of-field effects.

However, a larger maximum aperture does indeed let in more light—roughly two-thirds of a stop more. How much of a real difference that makes remains to be seen, but in theory it should allow for shorter exposure times in Night mode. I use this feature often—usually handheld—so I'm very much looking forward to trying it out.

Pro-grade camera controls

Being able to control shutter speed will definitely be useful for those frames where you're following a subject. Full white balance control will also be very useful. And I expect the histogram will come in very handy when manually adjusting exposure.

I generally don't care much for filters, whether applied at the time of shooting or later adjusted on the iPhone—I prefer traditional adjustment methods. So I rarely use the existing Photographic Styles, and I don't expect to use this latest version much more either. But I have to admit, its film presets are really tempting, so I'll definitely give them a try.

One of the biggest weaknesses of autofocus when shooting video is that when a subject is briefly occluded by another object, the camera may shift focus to that occluding object. Intelligent subject tracking claims to solve precisely this problem, so I will definitely put it through its paces.

Cinematic mode on standard video

I'm looking forward to hearing your views after you've used the 18 Pro for a while. I myself should probably upgrade—I'm still using the 12 Mini. (Mini, rest in peace.)

The telephoto lens is going to be a surprise; it might just make me accept a phone that's that much heavier and bigger than the Mini. I'm now weighing whether to pay the full $1,200 for a new 18 Pro, or get a used 16 Pro for around $700 or less—which is roughly what secondhand prices are like right now.

(The prices for the 17 Pro and 18 Pro are still fairly close, so I'm not considering the 17 Pro—I'd rather pay a little more and just get the 18 Pro outright.)

So if you feel the 18 Pro offers a significant improvement over the 16 Pro in the areas you mentioned, I'd love to hear your thoughts. Thanks!

Just under two months ago I said that Apple seemed to have given up on Cinematic video mode. I noted at the time that this was a real shame, because if Cinematic video were done well, it would be a killer feature for anyone wanting to use an iPhone as a more serious filmmaking tool. For a long time, it's almost done it, but always fallen just short; always a little bit off.

It turns out I was wrong: one of the new features of the iPhone 18 is the ability to apply Cinematic video effects to standard-mode footage.

The convenience of not having to decide in advance whether to use the mode is welcome, but what interests me most is that Apple appears to be reinvesting in doing this feature well. That means they've put in the work, so you can expect it to keep improving, much like Portrait mode did in its early days. I can't wait to try it out.

Those are the features I think will make the biggest difference for me personally. What about you? If you've already upgraded to the iPhone 18 Pro, which features compelled you to make the jump? Feel free to share in the comments.
